# The Harbour of Quiet Stars

## The Light Beyond the Harbour

Chapter 1 began with a small certainty: the tide would turn.

“Did you hear the bell?” Ivo asked. “It rang twice, and the tower has been empty since winter.” Mara looked at the water. “Then someone has come back.” He did not answer at once. Behind them, a shutter opened and closed, as if the house itself had decided to listen. Neither of them wished to be the first to walk away. On that visit she counted 100 stones before she stopped.

She remembered the instructions: *wait for the light, count the windows, and never mistake a reflection for a signal*. The words had seemed theatrical when she was a child. Here, with the salt wind pulling at the seams of her coat, they felt like ordinary advice. She counted seven windows. The eighth was a patch of darkness where a room should have been. On that visit she counted 101 stones before she stopped.

There was no hidden mechanism in the desk, no key beneath the loose board, and no message in the old ledger. Instead she found a pressed leaf between two blank pages. It had kept its colour through all those silent years. The smallest things survived, she thought, because nobody expected them to explain themselves. She placed the leaf carefully beside the chart. On that visit she counted 102 stones before she stopped.

“We can leave now,” he said. “There is still time.” She tightened the ribbon around the letters. “There is always time to leave. I want to know whether there is time to stay.” For a moment they watched the sky brighten above the warehouses. A gull settled on the rail, shook the rain from its wings, and waited with them. On that visit she counted 103 stones before she stopped.

The corridor narrowed where the builders had worked around the old stone. A person carrying a lantern would have had to turn sideways. Mara went slowly, one hand against the wall, feeling the marks left by tools whose names she did not know. At the far end, a rectangle of pale light rested on the floor. It was enough to keep her moving. On that visit she counted 104 stones before she stopped.

The rain had left a silver line along the harbour wall. Mara followed it until the lamps of the ferry station appeared through the mist. Every evening the keeper promised that the boat would return; every morning another empty rope lay against the stones. She carried the folded chart inside her coat, close enough to hear the paper move when she breathed. On that visit she counted 105 stones before she stopped.

“Did you hear the bell?” Ivo asked. “It rang twice, and the tower has been empty since winter.” Mara looked at the water. “Then someone has come back.” He did not answer at once. Here, with the salt wind pulling at the seams of her coat, they felt like ordinary advice. She counted seven windows. The eighth was a patch of darkness where a room should have been. On that visit she counted 107 stones before she stopped.

“We can leave now,” he said. “There is still time.” She tightened the ribbon around the letters. “There is always time to leave. I want to know whether there is time to stay.” For a moment they watched the sky brighten above the warehouses. A gull settled on the rail, shook the rain from its wings, and waited with them. On that visit she counted 808 stones before she stopped.

The corridor narrowed where the builders had worked around the old stone. A person carrying a lantern would have had to turn sideways. Mara went slowly, one hand against the wall, feeling the marks left by tools whose names she did not know. At the far end, a rectangle of pale light rested on the floor. It was enough to keep her moving. On that visit she counted 809 stones before she stopped.

The rain had left a silver line along the harbour wall. Mara followed it until the lamps of the ferry station appeared through the mist. Every evening the keeper promised that the boat would return; every morning another empty rope lay against the stones. She carried the folded chart inside her coat, close enough to hear the paper move when she breathed. On that visit she counted 810 stones before she stopped.

“Did you hear the bell?” Ivo asked. “It rang twice, and the tower has been empty since winter.” Mara looked at the water. “Then someone has come back.” He did not answer at once. Behind them, a shutter opened and closed, as if the house itself had decided to listen. Neither of them wished to be the first to walk away. On that visit she counted 811 stones before she stopped.

She remembered the instructions: *wait for the light, count the windows, and never mistake a reflection for a signal*. The words had seemed theatrical when she was a child. Here, with the salt wind pulling at the seams of her coat, they felt like ordinary advice. She counted seven windows. The eighth was a patch of darkness where a room should have been. On that visit she counted 812 stones before she stopped.

There was no hidden mechanism in the desk, no key beneath the loose board, and no message in the old ledger. Instead she found a pressed leaf between two blank pages. It had kept its colour through all those silent years. The smallest things survived, she thought, because nobody expected them to explain themselves. She placed the leaf carefully beside the chart. On that visit she counted 813 stones before she stopped.
